title: “FORGIVE AND YOU WILL BE FORGIVEN” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’RE STILL BLEEDING FROM WHAT THEY DID?
paragraphs: “FORGIVE AND YOU WILL BE FORGIVEN” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’RE STILL BLEEDING FROM WHAT THEY DID?

Did Jesus Really Make God’s Forgiveness Conditional on Yours? The Terrifying Warning, the Beautiful Gospel, and the Truth About Grace That Could Change How You See God, Your Wounds, and the People Who Broke You.
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that has kept some Christians awake at night.
Not because they don't love God.
Not because they refuse to obey Him.
But because somewhere in their past is a person whose name still makes their stomach tighten.
Someone who betrayed them.
Someone who destroyed their trust.
Someone who walked away without apologizing.
Someone who inflicted damage that cannot be undone with a simple conversation.
And then, one Sunday morning, they hear these words from Jesus:
“Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.” — Luke 6:37 (KJV)
Suddenly, their heart sinks.
What if I haven't forgiven them enough?
What if I say I've forgiven them, but the memories still hurt?
What if I die tonight with bitterness somewhere inside me?
Will God refuse to forgive me?
And perhaps the most frightening question of all:
Does this mean the blood of Jesus is not enough unless I successfully forgive everyone who has hurt me?

Read carefully, because the answer is more beautiful than cheap reassurance, more serious than popular Christianity sometimes admits, and far more Christ-centered than the idea that you must somehow purchase God's mercy with your own.
But before we reach that answer, we need to confront something uncomfortable.
Jesus did not say these words accidentally.
He did not misunderstand grace.
And He was not exaggerating simply to make His sermon memorable.
When the Son of God warned us about unforgiveness, He meant for us to listen.
The question is not whether His warning matters.
The question is whether we have understood what He was actually warning us about.
And the difference could change everything.
Imagine a woman sitting alone in her car after church.
The sermon was about forgiveness.
Everyone around her seemed encouraged.
Some nodded.
Some whispered amen.
But she sat behind the steering wheel, unable to turn the key.
Because the preacher said, “If you cannot forgive, God cannot forgive you.”
And immediately she remembered her father.
The father who was supposed to protect her.
The father whose cruelty had shaped years of her life.
The father who had never admitted what he did.
She had prayed about it.
She had cried about it.
She had tried to let go.
Some days she felt free.
Other days, one familiar voice or unexpected memory brought everything rushing back.
Now she wondered whether her salvation depended on achieving an emotional peace she could not manufacture.
She whispered through tears:
“Jesus, I want to forgive. But why does it still hurt?”
If that question sounds familiar, this article is for you.
And if you have been using God's forgiveness as permission to remain bitter, this article is also for you.
Because the Gospel comforts the wounded without excusing hatred.
It confronts the unforgiving without turning salvation into a wage.
And it brings both to the same place.
The cross of Jesus Christ.
Let's begin where Jesus actually spoke.
In Luke 6:36–37, Christ says:
“Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful. Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.”
Notice what comes before the command to forgive.
“Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.”
The Father's mercy is the pattern.
Jesus is teaching His disciples to reflect the character of the God they call Father.
In the Greek text, the command translated “forgive” in Luke 6:37 is ἀπολύετε (apolyete), from apolyō.

The word can mean to release, dismiss, set free, or let go. In this context, paired with commands against judging and condemning, it carries the sense of releasing others from condemnation and extending forgiveness.
The corresponding promise is ἀπολυθήσεσθε (apolythēsesthe), “you will be released” or, in this context, “you will be forgiven.”
That matters.
But we must be careful.

The Greek word does not magically settle every theological question about divine forgiveness. It does not, by itself, prove that forgiving someone erases all consequences or that a wounded person must immediately restore a dangerous relationship.
Words receive their meaning from context.
And here, Jesus is calling His people away from a condemning spirit and toward the mercy of their Father.
He is not teaching victims to pretend evil never happened.
He is teaching His disciples that mercy must become visible in the way they treat others.
But then we encounter an even stronger warning.
In Matthew 6:14–15, immediately after teaching the Lord's Prayer, Jesus declares:
“For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.”
There it is.
No comfortable escape.
No honest interpretation can simply remove those words.
Jesus explicitly connects our forgiveness of others with the Father's forgiveness of us.
The Greek verb used here is related to ἀφίημι (aphiēmi), meaning to send away, release, remit, or forgive.
In the Lord's Prayer, the word for debts is ὀφειλήματα (opheilēmata), while Matthew 6:14–15 speaks of παραπτώματα (paraptōmata), trespasses or offenses.
The language evokes the cancellation of a debt.
Something real was owed.
Something wrong was done.
And forgiveness involves relinquishing the claim to personal vengeance.
But does that mean we earn God's forgiveness by first forgiving other people?
No. Scripture does not teach that sinners can earn salvation by performing an act of forgiveness.
And the reason is not complicated.
It is the very foundation of the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Read those words again.
Not of yourselves.
The gift of God.
Not of works.
If forgiveness of other people were a meritorious payment that purchased salvation, then salvation would no longer be entirely a gift of grace.
It would become a transaction.
You forgive three people.
God forgives three hundred sins.
You release your enemies.
God releases you.
Your obedience becomes the price.
But that is not how the apostles preached salvation.
Romans 3:24 says that believers are:
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek word translated “freely” is δωρεάν (dōrean), conveying the idea of something given without payment or earned merit.
And the word for grace, χάρις (charis), speaks of favor or gift.
Paul is not describing a spiritual marketplace.
He is describing redemption grounded in Jesus Christ.
We are not justified because our forgiveness is perfect.
We are justified by God's grace through the redemption accomplished by Christ.
Yet here is where many explanations stop too soon.
They say, “Salvation is by grace, so unforgiveness doesn't really matter.”
But Jesus never said that.
And neither did Paul.
The same passage that tells us salvation is not earned by works also tells us in Ephesians 2:10 that believers are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
It saves us from sin's condemnation and begins transforming our relationship with sin itself.
That includes bitterness.
That includes vengeance.
That includes the secret satisfaction we sometimes feel imagining the downfall of someone who wounded us.
And if we are going to understand Jesus honestly, we cannot ignore the parable He told about a man who was forgiven an enormous debt but refused to forgive a much smaller one.
Matthew 18:21–35.
Peter approaches Jesus with a question that sounds generous.
How often should he forgive someone who sins against him?
Seven times?
Jesus responds:
“I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.” — Matthew 18:22
The point is not to establish a new numerical limit.
Jesus is dismantling the mindset that treats forgiveness as something we can carefully ration while maintaining a ledger of offenses.
Then He tells a story.
A servant owes his king ten thousand talents.
An almost unimaginable amount.
In the first-century setting, a talent represented an enormous monetary value. Ten thousand talents communicated a debt vastly beyond an ordinary servant's ability to repay.
The servant cannot pay.
Judgment approaches.
He falls before the king and begs for patience.
And the king does something astonishing.
He forgives the debt.
Not because the servant earned it.
Not because he offered a credible repayment plan.
But because the king was moved with compassion.
The servant walks away free.
Imagine that moment.
The terror lifting.
The impossible burden disappearing.
The future opening again.
But then something horrifying happens.
The forgiven servant finds a fellow servant who owes him one hundred denarii.
A real debt.
Not imaginary.
Not insignificant.
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer, so this was not pocket change.
But compared with ten thousand talents, it was tiny.
And instead of extending mercy, the forgiven servant grabs the man and demands repayment.
The other servant falls down and begs for patience.
The very posture the first servant had taken before the king.
The very plea he himself had made.
But he refuses.
He has the man imprisoned.
And when the king hears what happened, he confronts him:
“O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” — Matthew 18:32–33
Then comes the terrifying conclusion.
The king delivers him to the tormentors until the debt is paid.
Jesus ends by warning that His heavenly Father will likewise deal with those who refuse to forgive their brothers from their hearts.
We cannot make that warning disappear.
It is severe.
It is deliberate.
And it is meant to expose something spiritually deadly.
The servant wanted mercy as a benefit, but rejected mercy as a way of life.
He wanted his own debt erased while keeping his neighbor imprisoned.
He loved being released.
He did not love the mercy that released him.
And that is where the parable turns its gaze toward us.
Because it is possible to enjoy religious language about grace while refusing to let grace challenge the hatred we cherish.
It is possible to sing about the cross while quietly feeding fantasies of revenge.
It is possible to say “God knows my heart” when the very thing we are protecting from God is our heart.
Jesus is not teaching us how to purchase the King's compassion.
He is showing us how grotesquely inconsistent it is to claim the King's mercy while defiantly withholding mercy from others.
The warning is real.
A settled, unrepentant refusal to forgive is not a harmless personality trait.
It is a serious spiritual danger.
Christians have differed over how exactly Matthew 18 relates to final judgment, assurance of salvation, and the distinction between God's fatherly discipline and His saving forgiveness.
But across those discussions, one central truth remains difficult to evade.
The grace that forgives us also calls us to become forgiving people.
Our forgiveness does not purchase the cross.
The cross is the reason we are called to forgive.
Colossians 3:13 says:
“Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.”
Notice the order.
As Christ forgave you.
So also do ye.
Ephesians 4:32 says the same:
“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.”
This is not a small theological detail.
It changes the entire emotional center of obedience.
The Gospel does not say:
“Forgive perfectly, and perhaps Jesus will finally love you.”
It says:
“Look at the mercy God has shown you in Christ. Now, by His grace, learn to extend mercy to others.”
And that brings us to something many wounded believers desperately need to hear.
Forgiveness is not the same thing as pretending you were never hurt.
You can forgive someone and still remember what happened.
You can forgive someone and still experience grief.
You can forgive someone and still need distance.
You can forgive someone and still pursue justice.
You can forgive someone without trusting them again.
And you can forgive someone without giving them unrestricted access to your life.
The Bible never commands us to call evil good.
Isaiah 5:20 warns against confusing good and evil.
Romans 12:19 commands believers not to take personal vengeance, but that same chapter also tells us to pursue peace if it is possible, and as much as lies within us.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes a legitimate role for governing authorities in restraining and punishing wrongdoing.
Forgiveness does not abolish accountability.
It does not require a victim to conceal abuse.
It does not mean a person must return to an unsafe home, expose children to a dangerous individual, or abandon appropriate legal protection.
And reconciliation is not identical to forgiveness.
Reconciliation ordinarily requires the rebuilding of trust, and trust may require truthfulness, repentance, accountability, changed behavior, and time.
Sometimes reconciliation is not presently possible.
Sometimes it is not safe.
You may relinquish personal vengeance while still telling the truth about what happened.
You may pray for someone's repentance while refusing to enable their destruction of other people.
You may desire their ultimate good before God while recognizing that their present behavior makes closeness unwise.
That is not necessarily bitterness.
That may be wisdom.
And to the person who has been told, “If you really forgave, you wouldn't still cry,” please hear this.
Pain is not automatically proof of unforgiveness.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Psalms are filled with faithful people crying out from grief, betrayal, and distress.
Psalm 55 describes the anguish of being betrayed by someone close.
The Bible does not require emotional numbness as evidence of spiritual maturity.
Forgiveness is a moral and spiritual response to wrongdoing, not a magical deletion of memory.
It may begin with a genuine decision to surrender vengeance to God, while the work of healing continues through prayer, wise support, and time.
For some wounds, especially deep trauma, that process can be long and uneven.
You may need to return to the same prayer again and again.
Not because Christ has failed you.
But because healing is not always instantaneous.
And there is a difference between someone struggling to forgive and someone determined never to forgive.
The struggling believer may say:
“Lord, I know You call me to forgive, but I am finding it painfully difficult. Please help me.”
The hardened heart says:
“I know what You command, but I refuse. I want to keep my hatred.”
Those are not the same posture.
One is bringing weakness into the light.
The other is defending darkness.
And Jesus knows the difference.
Remember the desperate father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
His imperfect faith did not prevent him from bringing his need to Jesus.
In the same way, a believer struggling to forgive can honestly pray:
“Lord, I want to obey You. Help me where my heart is still resisting.”
That prayer is not hypocrisy.
It can be the beginning of repentance.
But there is another person reading this who needs a different kind of confrontation.
You have not merely been wounded.
You have become attached to your bitterness.
You replay the offense because anger makes you feel powerful.
You revisit the humiliation because hatred feels safer than vulnerability.
You tell yourself you have moved on, but secretly you are waiting for the day their life falls apart.
You do not simply want justice.
You want to watch them suffer.
And somewhere along the way, the person who hurt you became the center of your inner life.
They may have stopped thinking about you years ago.
But you still carry them into your mornings.
Into your marriage.
Into your prayers.
Into your conversations.
Into your sleep.
The wound was real.
The injustice was real.
But now bitterness is demanding a place in your heart that belongs to God.
Hebrews 12:15 warns about a root of bitterness springing up and causing trouble, defiling many.
The image is powerful.
A root begins beneath the surface.
Hidden.
Unnoticed.
But eventually it grows.
And what was once buried begins affecting everything around it.
That is what unresolved bitterness can do.
It can make innocent people pay for someone else's sin.
It can make love feel threatening.
It can turn healthy correction into perceived betrayal.
It can make us suspicious of kindness.
And it can cause us to become harsh in ways that resemble the very people who wounded us.
This is not inevitable, and wounded people should never be blamed for the wrong committed against them.
But the danger is real.
Unforgiveness can extend the reach of an old injury into places where the original offender no longer has any rightful authority.
Jesus calls us out of that bondage.
Not by denying the wrong.
Not by excusing the offender.
But by teaching us to entrust judgment to God.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Forgiveness does not mean the universe has forgotten what happened.
It means you are no longer claiming the throne of final judgment.
God sees.
God knows.
God is just.
And because He is just, you do not have to become consumed with administering ultimate justice yourself.
But how can we trust that?
How can a holy God forgive sinners without treating sin as though it does not matter?
How can He command mercy without becoming indifferent to evil?
The answer stands outside Jerusalem.
At a place called Golgotha.
And here the entire story changes.
Because Christianity does not teach that God simply shrugged at human wickedness.
It teaches that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
The Hebrew phrase מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ (meḥolal mippeshaʿenu) communicates that the Servant was pierced or wounded because of our transgressions.
And מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ (medukkaʾ meʿavonoteinu) speaks of His being crushed because of our iniquities.
These are not descriptions of a God who takes evil lightly.
They point to the costliness of redemption.
Christ did not suffer because sin was unimportant.
He suffered because sin is deadly serious, and because God's saving love is astonishingly deep.
The New Testament identifies Jesus with the suffering Servant, and 1 Peter 2:24 declares:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.”
There is the Gospel.
Jesus bears our sins.
Jesus gives Himself.
Jesus makes redemption possible.
And through Him, sinners are called to repent, believe, and receive God's grace.
Then, while hanging on the cross, Jesus speaks words that still confront the human heart.
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34
This saying appears in the traditional text reflected in the King James Version, though some early Greek manuscripts omit it. The textual question deserves acknowledgment rather than concealment.
Its portrayal of Jesus' mercy is consistent with His teaching to love enemies and with the wider New Testament witness.
Look at the scene.
Christ is being crucified.
He is not surrounded by people who have carefully earned His kindness.
He is being mocked and brutalized.
And He prays for forgiveness.
The Greek phrase is:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς (Pater, aphes autois).
“Father, forgive them.”
The verb ἄφες (aphes) comes from the same Greek verb family, aphiēmi, that appears in Matthew's teaching about forgiveness.
The One who commanded forgiveness also embodied mercy under suffering.
Yet we must not twist this into a claim that every person involved in the crucifixion was automatically saved without repentance or faith.
The prayer reveals Christ's merciful heart; it does not erase the New Testament's call to repentance and belief.
But what a heart it reveals.
And what a Savior.
The One who has every right to judge is also the One who gave Himself to save.
The One who exposes our sin is the One who offers cleansing.
The One who commands us to forgive is the One who supplies grace to change us.
That is why forgiveness is not ultimately about proving that we are strong enough.
It is about being transformed by someone infinitely stronger than our sin.
Now consider one more scene.
Not a crucifixion.
A breakfast.
A charcoal fire.
A conversation beside the Sea of Galilee.
Peter had denied Jesus three times.
Not privately in his thoughts.
Not merely through a moment of confusion.
He had publicly disowned the Lord he claimed he would never abandon.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked upon Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine the weight of that memory.
The sound of his own denial.
The rooster crowing.
The eyes of Jesus.
The shame.
Then, after the resurrection, John 21 records Jesus speaking with Peter.
Three times Jesus asks whether Peter loves Him.
And three times Peter is given the opportunity to respond.
Jesus commissions him to care for His sheep.
Peter's failure was not declared harmless.
His denial was not rewritten as courage.
But neither was his failure the final word.
The risen Christ restored him to service.
That is the heart of our theme.
Not because He changes the historical truth of our sin.
Not because He pretends betrayal never happened.
But because His grace can give a repentant sinner a future that guilt alone could never produce.
Peter's story did not end with denial.
It continued through the mercy and calling of Jesus.
And your story does not have to end with what someone did to you.
Or what you did to someone else.
Or the bitterness you have been carrying.
Or the guilt you have been hiding.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is repentance.
There is restoration.
There is a new way to live.
And perhaps you are finally beginning to see why Jesus' warning about forgiveness matters so much.
He is not inviting us to earn salvation by becoming morally impressive.
He is exposing the contradiction of wanting divine mercy while permanently rejecting mercy toward others.
He is calling us to turn from the very sin that would keep us spiritually hardened.
He is teaching us to live as people who have encountered grace.
And He is directing our attention away from our ability to save ourselves and toward the Savior who alone can redeem us.
But what about the Christian who is terrified that one remaining struggle with resentment means God has rejected them?
Look at 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And look at Romans 8:1:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The promise is not that believers never struggle.
The promise is that those who belong to Christ are not left to face condemnation apart from Him.
When the Holy Spirit exposes unforgiveness, the answer is not to run away from Jesus in terror.
It is to come to Jesus in repentance.
Confess the bitterness.
Confess the desire for revenge.
Confess the fear.
Confess the inability to manufacture warm feelings toward someone who has caused enormous pain.
Ask for His help.
And take the next faithful step.
Maybe that step is to stop rehearsing revenge.
Maybe it is to pray that the person who hurt you would genuinely repent.
Maybe it is to stop spreading unnecessary stories designed to humiliate them.
Maybe it is to establish a boundary you should have established years ago.
Maybe it is to seek wise pastoral care or professional support because the trauma remains overwhelming.
Maybe it is to admit that you have been calling something “discernment” when it has really become contempt.
Or maybe, for the first time, you simply need to whisper:
“Jesus, I cannot heal this by myself.”
That is not the end of faith.
That can be the beginning of surrender.
And do not miss this distinction.
Forgiveness is not saying, “What you did was acceptable.”
Forgiveness is saying, “What you did was wrong, but I will not make personal vengeance the master of my life.”
Forgiveness is not saying, “You deserve my trust.”
It is saying, “I will not allow hatred to dictate my obedience to Christ.”
Forgiveness is not saying, “There should be no consequences.”
It is saying, “I will entrust ultimate justice to God while pursuing what is right.”
And forgiveness is certainly not saying, “I am now responsible for making the offender feel comfortable.”
The call to forgive never makes you responsible for another person's refusal to repent.
It calls you to faithfulness before God.
There is also a danger on the opposite side.
Some people are so afraid of sounding legalistic that they turn forgiveness into an optional spiritual preference.
They treat Jesus' warnings as though they were merely inspirational suggestions.
But the same Lord who welcomes the weary also commands His followers to forgive.
Grace is free.
Discipleship is costly.
Those truths are not enemies.
Jesus saves us by grace, and that grace teaches us to renounce sin.
Titus 2:11–12 describes the grace of God as bringing salvation and teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is God's undeserved favor at work in people who could never transform themselves.
And sometimes its work is painful.
Because forgiving may mean surrendering the imaginary conversation in which you finally humiliate the person who humiliated you.
It may mean accepting that you will never receive the apology you deserved.
It may mean grieving the childhood you cannot recover.
It may mean acknowledging that your marriage, friendship, family, or ministry will never look exactly as it did before the betrayal.
It may mean letting God deal with someone whose repentance you cannot control.
And that surrender can feel like losing.
Until you begin to realize what bitterness has been costing you.
Not because forgiveness guarantees that all emotional pain will disappear.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored.
But because Christ is teaching you to live without surrendering your soul to revenge.
That is freedom of a different kind.
A freedom that does not depend on your offender's cooperation.
A freedom rooted in belonging to Jesus.
And now I want to speak to the person who has never truly come to Christ.
You may have read this far thinking about someone you need to forgive.
But there is a deeper question.
Have you received the forgiveness of God through Jesus Christ?
Not merely admired Christian morality.
Not merely attended church.
Not merely posted Bible verses.
Have you turned to Christ in repentance and faith?
Because the greatest debt in this story is not the debt another human being owes you.
It is the debt of sin that no amount of religious performance can erase.
Romans 6:23 declares:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
And Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had achieved perfect emotional health.
Not after we had performed enough acts of forgiveness to qualify for mercy.
Christ died for sinners.
And the risen Jesus calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
This is not an invitation to remain comfortable in sin.
It is an invitation to come out of hiding.
To stop defending what God calls evil.
To stop trying to save yourself.
To entrust yourself to the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you already belong to Him, then bring your unfinished struggle with forgiveness into His light.
Do not mistake conviction for abandonment.
The Lord who calls you to repentance is not calling you away from grace.
He is calling you deeper into it.
There is a beautiful picture of forgiveness in the Old Testament.
Psalm 103:12 says:
“As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.”
In Hebrew, the key phrase is:
כִּרְחֹק מִזְרָח מִמַּעֲרָב (kirḥoq mizraḥ mimmaʿarav)
“As far as east is from west.”
The image communicates extraordinary distance.
God's mercy is described through the removal of transgressions from those who fear Him.
It does not mean God has become ignorant of history.
It means He mercifully removes the guilt of sin.
And through the fuller revelation of the Gospel, we see that the forgiveness of sins is accomplished through Jesus Christ.
Acts 13:38 declares:
“Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins.”
Through this man.
Jesus.
Not through our perfect performance.
Not through religious payments.
Not through emotional self-punishment.
Through Jesus Christ.
A donation cannot replace repentance.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, worship, and lives transformed by His grace.
One beautiful way to express that generosity is to help faithful Gospel ministry continue.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply.
Giving should never be driven by fear that God will withhold His love unless we pay.
And it should never be forced by guilt.

In Scripture, tithes and offerings belong to the wider story of worship and stewardship. Christians differ in their understanding of how Old Testament tithing applies under the New Covenant, but the New Testament clearly commends willing, generous, proportionate support for the work of the Gospel.
Behind every article is a simple hope.
That someone who feels too sinful to come home will discover the mercy of Christ.
That someone trapped in bitterness will begin surrendering it to Jesus.
That someone wounded by religion will encounter the truth of Scripture rather than manipulation.
That someone on the edge of giving up will hear the Gospel and find a reason to seek the Lord again.
And that someone who has spent years hiding behind a smile will finally have the courage to say, “I need prayer.”
That is the kind of work your voluntary support can help continue and expand.
These resources are intended to help you move beyond a moment of inspiration into sustained biblical learning, prayer, and discipleship.
Because spiritual growth is not built on one emotional article.
It grows through a life continually shaped by the Word of God.
Not because Jesus needs you to buy His love.
Not because your salvation depends on a monthly payment.
But because Gospel ministry is worth supporting freely, prayerfully, and joyfully when you believe in its mission and have the means to do so.
Someone who thinks their past has permanently disqualified them.
Someone who has been told that their inability to instantly forget trauma means they are a bad Christian.
Someone whose bitterness is slowly destroying their peace.
Someone who needs to hear both the seriousness of Jesus' warning and the sufficiency of His grace.
And please, do not leave this conversation without allowing the Word to search your own heart.
What is harder for you right now: believing that God has forgiven you, or learning to forgive someone who hurt you?
You do not need to expose private details or name the person who wounded you.
Your words may encourage someone who is only beginning that journey.
No one has to disclose trauma publicly to prove faith, and a comment is never a condition of receiving God's grace.
But honest testimony can remind other believers that they are not walking alone.
And now, before you go, return to the question that brought us here.
“Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
Does that mean God's forgiveness is earned by forgiving others?
No.
Forgiveness is not the currency with which we purchase salvation.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
His atoning death and resurrection are the foundation of our hope.
Salvation is received by grace through faith, not earned by works.
But does that mean we can cling defiantly to unforgiveness without spiritual consequence?
Also no.
Jesus' warnings are too clear for that.
A heart that persistently rejects mercy while claiming to possess it has reason for serious self-examination.
The right response is not self-salvation through moral effort.
It is repentance and renewed dependence on Christ.
We do not forgive others to make the cross sufficient. We forgive because the sufficient Savior calls His redeemed people to reflect His mercy.
And when we fail, we do not hide.
We confess.
We repent.
We ask for grace.
We keep following Jesus.
Perhaps the person who wounded you will never apologize.
Perhaps they will never understand the damage.
Perhaps they will continue telling a version of the story in which they did nothing wrong.
You cannot control their repentance.
You cannot force their honesty.
You cannot manufacture reconciliation.
But you can bring your wounded heart before the Lord who sees everything.
You can refuse to make revenge your master.
You can seek justice without surrendering to hatred.
You can learn to forgive without denying the truth.
And you can trust that the God who commands mercy is also the God who gives grace to help His people obey.
Maybe tonight you are not ready to say, “I have completely let go.”
Then begin with something honest.
“Jesus, I want to want what You want.”
Maybe tomorrow the memory will hurt again.
Bring it to Him again.
Maybe next month you will discover another layer of resentment you did not know was there.
Confess it.
Surrender it.
Keep walking.
And remember that the deepest miracle of forgiveness is not that wounded human beings suddenly become incapable of feeling pain.
It is that Jesus Christ can teach wounded human beings to live in His mercy without allowing the wrong done to them to define the whole of their lives.
The scandal of sin is real.
The devastation of betrayal is real.
The command to forgive is real.
The warning against an unforgiving heart is real.
But so is the empty tomb.
So is the risen Savior.
So is the promise of grace.
So is the transforming power of the Holy Spirit.
And so is the hope that your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
If you need words to begin, pray this from your heart:

“Lord Jesus, You know what happened. You know what they did. You know what I did. You know the wounds I hide and the resentment I sometimes defend. I confess that I cannot save myself, and I cannot transform my heart apart from Your grace. Thank You for giving Yourself for sinners and rising again. Forgive my sins. Teach me to forgive without pretending evil is good. Give me wisdom to establish righteous boundaries, courage to seek justice rightly, humility to repent where I have sinned, and strength to release personal vengeance into Your hands. Where I am hardened, soften me. Where I am frightened, sustain me. Where I am wounded, help me heal. And where I have forgotten the mercy You have shown me, bring me back to the cross. Let my life testify not to my own goodness, but to the transforming grace of Jesus Christ. Amen.”
And when you close this article, I hope you remember something greater than the person who betrayed you.
Greater than the sin you regret.
Greater than the anger you have struggled to surrender.
Remember the Savior who did not wait for sinners to become worthy before giving Himself for them.
Remember that His grace is not an excuse to remain in darkness.
It is the invitation to come into the light.
And remember that when Jesus rewrites a life, He does not need to pretend the painful pages never existed.
He redeems people whose stories are full of them.
The hands that were pierced for your forgiveness are the same hands you can trust with the wounds you are still learning to release.
